1.note: Here Yahweh is speaking as if the earth were **the stool of my feet**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I rule over the earth as easily as I rest my feet on a stool]

1.q: אֵי זֶ֥ה בַ֨יִת֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר תִּבְנוּ לִ֔⁠י וְ⁠אֵי זֶ֥ה מָק֖וֹם מְנוּחָתִֽ⁠י
1.note: Yahweh is using the question form to emphasize that no house any human could build would ever be able to contain him or serve as his resting place. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [There is no suitable house that you could build for me, and there is no place that could be my rest!]

2.note: Here, **my hand** represents Yahweh’s power. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [my power has made]

Isaiah is using **the declaration of Yahweh** to indicate that what has been said is a direct quotation from Yahweh and comes with Yahweh’s authority. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language.

Yahweh is using **trembling at my word** as a common expression of the culture to mean “showing deep reverence for and obeying what I say.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and who deeply revere and obey what I say]

The terms **humble** and **contrite of spirit** mean similar things. Isaiah is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [people who are truly humble and lowly in spirit]

3.note: Here Yahweh is speaking of a person who continues to sin while he sacrifices an ox as if that person were **striking a man**, that is, committing murder. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The one slaughtering an ox while continuing to sin is as guilty as one committing murder]

Here Yahweh is speaking of a person who sacrifices a lamb while continuing to sin as if that person were **breaking the neck** of a dog, an unclean and detestable act. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the one sacrificing a lamb while continuing to sin is doing something as detestable to me as sacrificing a dog]

Here Yahweh is speaking of a person who presents a grain offering while continuing to sin as if that person were offering **the blood of a pig**, something abominable and forbidden. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the one bringing up a grain offering while continuing to sin is as guilty as one offering the blood of a pig]

Here, **nothingness** represents an idol, which has no real existence or power. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [is worshiping an idol that has no power]

Yahweh is stating the pronoun **they** separately, even though the verb translated as **they have chosen** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that the people themselves are the ones who have chosen their own sinful ways. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [They themselves have chosen their ways]

4.note: Yahweh is stating the pronoun **I** separately, even though the verb translated as **I will choose** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that he himself, in contrast to the people who chose their own sinful ways, is the one choosing their punishment. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [I myself will choose their harsh treatments]

Here, **their fears** represents the very things that they are afraid of. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and I will bring on them the things they are afraid of]

Yahweh is using **in my eyes** as a common expression of the culture to mean “according to my judgment.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they did what I judge to be evil]

5.note: Here, **my name** represents Yahweh himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [for my sake]

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [that they want Yahweh to be glorious, that they might see your joy]

The people who hate Yahweh actually mean to communicate the opposite of the literal meaning of what they are saying here. If a speaker of your language would not do that, you could translate the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [We doubt that Yahweh will be glorious so that we will see your joy.]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **shame**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [they will be ashamed]

6.q: ק֤וֹל שָׁאוֹן֙ מֵ⁠עִ֔יר ק֖וֹל מֵֽ⁠הֵיכָ֑ל ק֣וֹל יְהוָ֔ה מְשַׁלֵּ֥ם גְּמ֖וּל לְ⁠אֹיְבָֽי⁠ו
6.note: Isaiah is using these phrases to express a strong feeling of alarm as Yahweh comes to punish his enemies. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [Listen! A roar is coming from the city! A sound is coming from the temple, the sound of Yahweh giving his enemies what they deserve]

6.q: ק֤וֹל שָׁאוֹן֙ מֵ⁠עִ֔יר ק֖וֹל מֵֽ⁠הֵיכָ֑ל ק֣וֹל יְהוָ֔ה מְשַׁלֵּ֥ם גְּמ֖וּל לְ⁠אֹיְבָֽי⁠ו
6.note: These three phrases mean basically the same thing. The second and third emphasize the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in poetry, and follow that approach here and throughout this chapter. Alternate translation: [Listen to the great commotion coming from the city, that same noise coming from the temple—it is the sound of Yahweh repaying his enemies for what they have done]

7.note: Here Isaiah is speaking of how the people of Zion will suddenly be restored as if a woman **births** a child before she even goes into labor. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Zion will be restored as suddenly as a woman who gives birth before she writhes in labor;]

8.q: מִֽי שָׁמַ֣ע כָּ⁠זֹ֗את מִ֤י רָאָה֙ כָּ⁠אֵ֔לֶּה
8.note: Isaiah is using the question form to emphasize that no one has ever heard of or seen anything like this before. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [No one has ever heard of anything like this! No one has ever seen anything like these!]

8.q: הֲ⁠י֤וּחַל אֶ֨רֶץ֙ בְּ⁠י֣וֹם אֶחָ֔ד אִם יִוָּ֥לֵֽד גּ֖וֹי פַּ֣עַם אֶחָ֑ת
8.note: Isaiah is using the question form to emphasize how astonishing it is that a whole nation could come into being in a single day or moment, something that would normally be impossible. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Surely a land cannot be writhed in one day! Surely a nation cannot be birthed in one moment!]

The expression **be writhed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Will a land writhe a nation in one day]
See how you translated the term “Or” in 10:9. Alternate translation: [Indeed,]

The expression **be birthed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [a nation appears] or [a nation comes forth]

Isaiah is speaking of **Zion** as if it were a woman who could give birth to children. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the people of Zion suddenly became a nation]

9.q: הַ⁠אֲנִ֥י אַשְׁבִּ֛יר וְ⁠לֹ֥א אוֹלִ֖יד יֹאמַ֣ר יְהוָ֑ה אִם־אֲנִ֧י הַ⁠מּוֹלִ֛יד וְ⁠עָצַ֖רְתִּי אָמַ֥ר אֱלֹהָֽיִ⁠ךְ
9.note: Yahweh is using the question form to emphasize that he will certainly finish the work he has begun, just as one who brings a mother to the point of delivery would not then prevent the birth. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I will surely break open and cause to birth. … I will surely not restrain.]
See how you translated the term “Or” in 10:9 and in the previous verse. Alternate translation: [Indeed,]

10.q: שִׂמְח֧וּ אֶת־יְרוּשָׁלִַ֛ם וְ⁠גִ֥ילוּ בָ֖⁠הּ כָּל־אֹהֲבֶ֑י⁠הָ שִׂ֤ישׂוּ אִתָּ⁠הּ֙ מָשׂ֔וֹשׂ כָּל־הַ⁠מִּֽתְאַבְּלִ֖ים עָלֶֽי⁠הָ
10.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in poetry, and follow that approach here and throughout this chapter. Alternate translation: [Rejoice with Jerusalem and be very glad for her, all you who love her; celebrate joyfully with her, all you who mourn over her]

11.note: Here Isaiah is speaking of the people receiving comfort and abundance from Jerusalem as if they were infants who **nurse** at the **breast of her consolations**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you may be fully comforted and satisfied by her]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **satisfaction**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [you may nurse and satisfy yourselves]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **abundance**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [from her abundant glory]

12.note: The point of this comparison is that just as a **river** flows abundantly and continuously, so is the **peace** that Yahweh extends to Jerusalem abundant and unceasing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [making her peace as abundant and unceasing as a flowing river]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **peace**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [causing her to be peaceful]

The point of this comparison is that just as an **overflowing stream** carries a great volume of water, so is the wealth that flows to Jerusalem great in abundance. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and as abundantly as an overflowing stream carries water]

Here, **the glory of the nations** represents the wealth and riches of the nations. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the wealth of the nations]

Here Yahweh is speaking of how Jerusalem will care for her people as if they were infants who would be **carried** on her side and **bounced** on her knees. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [She will tenderly care for you, holding you close and comforting you as a mother does her infant child]

The expression **be carried** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [She will carry you]

The expression **be bounced** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and she will bounce you up and down]

13.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **a man whose mother comforts him** is consoled and reassured, so Yahweh will comfort his people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [Just as a mother consoles and reassures her son]

The expression **be comforted** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and I will comfort you in Jerusalem]

14.note: Here the **heart** represents where a person’s feelings and emotions exist. You may have a comparable expression in your language, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and you will rejoice within yourself]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the grass** flourishes with fresh, green growth, so **your bones** will flourish with renewed health and strength. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and your bones will become healthy and strong, just as the grass flourishes with fresh growth]

The expression **be made known** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh will make his hand known]
Here, **the hand of Yahweh** represents Yahweh’s power. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the power of Yahweh]

15.note: Isaiah is using the term **behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Look]

Here Isaiah is speaking of Yahweh’s judgment as if it were **fire** that he brings with him. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [will come to bring judgment]

The phrase leaves out an implied verb for “his chariots,” to be understood from “will come” earlier in the sentence. Isaiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and his chariots will come like a windstorm]

The point of this comparison is that just as a **windstorm** moves with swift and overwhelming force, so Yahweh’s **chariots** will advance with unstoppable speed and power. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and his chariots will move with unstoppable speed and power]

Isaiah is using **his nose with heat** as a common expression of the culture to mean “intense anger.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to render his intense anger]

Isaiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and to render his rebuke in flames of fire]

16.note: Here, **his sword** represents violent attack. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and by violence]

Isaiah is using **all flesh** to represent all people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [all people]

Isaiah is using the adjective **slain** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [those whom Yahweh slays]

17.note: The implication is that these people are performing pagan worship rituals in gardens, following a leader who stands in their midst. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [to worship idols in the gardens, following the leader who stands among them]

Yahweh is referring to dying in a polite way by using the phrase **end together**. Depending on what is helpful for your readers, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language, or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [they will all die together]

18.note: Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [And I know their deeds and their thoughts]

Here, **languages** represents the people who speak those languages. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [all of the nations and the people who speak other languages]

19.q: תַּרְשִׁ֨ישׁ פּ֥וּל וְ⁠ל֛וּד מֹ֥שְׁכֵי קֶ֖שֶׁת תֻּבַ֣ל וְ⁠יָוָ֑ן
19.note: The words **Tarshish**, **Pul**, **Lud**, **Tubal**, and **Javan** are the names of distant places and the peoples who lived in them.

Isaiah is using **drawers of the bow** as a common expression of the culture to mean “archers,” soldiers who fight with bows and arrows. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [soldiers who shoot arrows]

20.note: Here the masculine term **brothers** has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [all of your brothers and sisters]
Here Yahweh refers to himself in the third person as **Yahweh**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [as an offering to me]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **holiness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [my holy mountain]

20.q: כַּ⁠אֲשֶׁ֣ר יָבִיאוּ֩ בְנֵ֨י יִשְׂרָאֵ֧ל אֶת הַ⁠מִּנְחָ֛ה בִּ⁠כְלִ֥י טָה֖וֹר
20.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **the sons of Israel bring the grain offering in a clean vessel** as a pure and acceptable gift, so the nations will bring the exiled Israelites back to Jerusalem as an acceptable offering to Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [as an acceptable gift, just as the sons of Israel bring the grain offering as a pure gift in a clean vessel]

22.q: כַ⁠אֲשֶׁ֣ר הַ⁠שָּׁמַ֣יִם הַ֠⁠חֳדָשִׁים וְ⁠הָ⁠אָ֨רֶץ הַ⁠חֲדָשָׁ֜ה אֲשֶׁ֨ר אֲנִ֥י עֹשֶׂ֛ה עֹמְדִ֥ים לְ⁠פָנַ֖⁠י
22.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **the new heavens and the new earth** that Yahweh is making will endure permanently before him, so the descendants and name of his people will endure permanently. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [just as the new heavens and the new earth that I am making will endure permanently before me … so your descendants and your name will endure permanently]
The word **your** is plural in both instances because it refers to the Israelites as a group, so use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

Here Yahweh is speaking of a person’s descendants as if they were **seed** that is planted and grows. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your descendants]

Here, **your name** represents your reputation and the lasting memory of you among future generations. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and your reputation]

23.note: Yahweh is using **from new moon to its new moon and from Sabbath to its Sabbath** as a common expression of the culture to mean “at every appointed time of worship, month after month and week after week.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [at every monthly new moon celebration and every weekly Sabbath]
Here, **my face** represents Yahweh’s presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to my presence]

24.q: תוֹלַעְתָּ֞⁠ם לֹ֣א תָמ֗וּת וְ⁠אִשָּׁ⁠ם֙ לֹ֣א תִכְבֶּ֔ה
24.note: Here Yahweh is speaking of the never-ending punishment of those who rebelled against him as if it were a **worm** that **will not die** and a **fire** that **will not go out**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [their punishment will never end]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **abhorrence**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and they will be detestable]
